planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into well-drained soil; patagua tolerates more sun, alkalinity, and summer dryness once established than its relative the Chilean lantern tree.

directions: Patagua is an evergreen tree of central Chile's river margins and coastal ranges, distinct from its better-known relative Crinodendron hookerianum in bearing small, waxy, white to pale pink bell-shaped flowers along its branches in summer rather than the pendulous red lanterns of the lantern tree. It develops a dense, glossy-leaved crown and in habitat and street-tree plantings in Chile can reach a substantial tree size, though in cultivated gardens outside its native range it is more often grown as a large shrub. It is notably more tolerant of heat, drier soil, and some lime than C. hookerianum, making it a useful substitute where woodland-garden conditions are not available. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil and water regularly while young to establish a deep root system.

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed into rich, well-drained soil with shelter from wind and strong midday sun.

directions: Luculia pinceana is a fragrant understory shrub native to the forests of Nepal, northeast India, and south into Yunnan and Myanmar, distinct from the more commonly grown Luculia gratissima in bearing smaller, looser flower clusters and in generally flowering later into the winter months. It is slightly more cold-tender than L. gratissima and benefits from a sheltered, frost-free or near frost-free site, or container culture with winter protection in marginal climates. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture and broken shade, since its soft foliage scorches readily in hot, exposed sun. Light pruning after flowering keeps the naturally loose, open habit tidy and encourages fresh flowering wood.

planting.note: Divide spreading rhizomes in spring and plant into permanently damp to waterlogged soil at a pond margin, ditch, or wet meadow bed.

directions: European hedge-hyssop is a low, rhizomatous perennial of wet meadows, ditches, and riverbanks across much of Europe, distinct from the smaller North American annual Gratiola neglecta already in this database. It carries narrow, opposite leaves and small tubular, two-lipped flowers that are whitish with pink to purple veining, borne singly in the leaf axils through summer. Historically it was gathered as a harsh folk-medicine purgative, but all parts are toxic if ingested in quantity and it should be treated strictly as an ornamental or conservation wetland plant, not a culinary or medicinal herb. In the garden it is used mainly by specialist native-plant and wildlife-pond nurseries to furnish permanently saturated soil at the shallow margins of ponds or bog gardens, where it has become uncommon in the wild in parts of its range and is valued for naturalistic wetland restoration plantings.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI)

planting.note: Sow as early as the ground can be worked, well before the last frost, since this early-maturing variety needs a cool start and finishes before summer heat sets in.

directions: Released in 1997 by the Crop Development Centre at the University of Saskatchewan, this brown-seeded oilseed flax became a long-standing benchmark variety against which newer Canadian prairie flax cultivars were measured for yield and maturity. Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into a firm, cool seedbed in early spring, since it germinates and establishes well before soil warms fully. It matures slightly earlier than many older flax types, a trait valued in short-season growing regions, and produces the same sky-blue flowers and rattling seed capsules typical of the species. Harvest once most bolls have browned and dried, then thresh and store the oily brown seed for cold-pressing into linseed oil.
sources: Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture flax variety performance guides
University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

planting.note: Sow in early spring on the same cool-season schedule as conventional flax; isolate plantings from other flax to keep the seed's distinct oil chemistry pure.

directions: Bred by CSIRO in Australia and marketed from the early 1990s under the Linola trade name, this is a 'solin' type flax selected to have very low alpha-linolenic acid and high linoleic acid, giving an edible oil that behaves more like sunflower or safflower oil than traditional flaxseed oil and resists going rancid. Field culture is identical to ordinary oilseed flax, sown shallowly into a firm, cool seedbed in earliest spring and harvested once the capsules dry and rattle, but growers keep it isolated from conventional flax fields because the seed is visually indistinguishable and commingling ruins the low-linolenic trait buyers pay for. The plant shows the same slender stems and pale blue flowers as other flax, maturing on a similar timeline. It is grown strictly for the edible-oil market rather than for fiber or omega-3-rich nutritional flaxseed.
sources: North Dakota State University Extension flax production guide

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost, since the taproot resents transplanting; a cut-flower selection bred for fewer spines on the bracts.

directions: This selection was developed specifically for cut-flower growers, with noticeably fewer spines along the bract edges than field-type safflower, making the stems far more comfortable to handle and bunch. Flower heads open a soft creamy yellow and deepen over several days to a rich saffron orange, giving a single planting two distinct color phases to harvest from. Sow seed directly where it will grow and thin to final spacing, since the deep taproot makes this plant a poor transplant candidate. Cut stems for arrangements as the bracts are just beginning to show color for the longest vase life, and expect strong, upright stems that hold up well in both fresh and dried bouquets.
sources: Floret Flower Farm cut-flower trial notes
